title: Listen to him (Mark 9:1–13)
hookLine: the transfiguration, and the one instruction from the cloud: listen to him
carry: let it change what you do

cards: Six days later, Mark says, Jesus takes three friends, Peter, James and John, up a high mountain, just the four of them. Up there, he changes in front of them.
His clothes turn shining, dazzling white, and Mark, who loves a homely detail, says they were whiter than any laundryman on earth could get them.
Then two figures appear, talking with him: Elijah and Moses, great prophets from centuries before. And Peter, bless him, has to say something. It's good for us to be here!
Let's build three shelters: one for you, one for Moses, one for Elijah. Mark adds, gently: "For he wist not what to say; for they were sore afraid." He didn't know what to say, so he said something.

teach.b: While Peter is still planning construction, a cloud comes down and covers them, and a voice speaks out of it. In the King James Bible: "This is my beloved Son: hear him." One sentence of introduction, one instruction.
Not build. Not explain. Hear him.
The Greek word means listen, and in the Bible listening is never just sound in the ears. In Hebrew, the same word covers hearing and obeying. To really listen is to let it change what you do.
Notice what the voice doesn't say: listen to Moses and Elijah too.

Many Christians read those two as standing for the Law and the Prophets, the whole Hebrew Bible, gathered around Jesus. Then, suddenly, they look around and see no one any more, only Jesus, with them.
The cloud and the glow are gone: an ordinary man on a mountain, and the instruction to listen.
Mark never names the mountain. Christian tradition since early centuries has pointed to Mount Tabor in Galilee, and others suggest Mount Hermon, much nearer Caesarea Philippi.
On the way down he tells them to tell no one until he has risen from the dead, and they puzzle over what that could mean.

teach.h: THIS IS MY BELOVED SON: HEAR HIM.
teach.b: Christians call this the transfiguration, from the Latin for being changed in form. Orthodox Christians hold it especially dear, and Catholic, Anglican and many other churches keep it as a feast on the sixth of August.

how: Many churches celebrate the Transfiguration as a feast, on August 6 in the Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican calendars, and many Protestant churches read the story on the Sunday before Lent; Christians often speak of listening to Jesus through reading the Gospels and in silent prayer.

o: a harvest festival held in the autumn
Jesus changed in form, shining on a mountain
a prayer said quietly before sleep

games.q: who's on the mountain — tap the pairs.

s: Mark names the mountain as Mount Tabor
Mark never names it. Tabor is later tradition; some suggest Mount Hermon.
"This is my beloved Son: hear him."

games.q: you're Peter, on the mountain. Jesus is shining, Moses and Elijah are beside him, and you are terrified. what do you do?
o: run down to tell the others.
games.why: Peter offers to build, "for he wist not what to say". the voice from the cloud answers with one word of instruction: hear him.

practice: Don't plan anything, don't fix anything, don't build any shelters: just listen, first to the sounds of the room, then to the sounds far away, then to the quiet underneath. If a thought wants to talk, let it pass like a cloud.
If you pray, you can hold the line hear him, and wait, without filling the silence.

wordCard.voice: Transfiguration, from Latin for being changed in form: the mountain where Jesus shone before Peter, James and John, and a voice said, listen.

orig.note: Greek: listen, hear (said to more than one person). the word from the cloud in Mark 9:7.

carryVoice: Your line: let it change what you do. The voice gave one instruction: hear him. Day one hundred ninety-five, complete.
